facts.label: Approaching
facts.value: Heading toward us at ~110 km/s; merger with the Milky Way in ~4-5 billion years

M31.about: The nearest big galaxy and the most distant thing most people can see with the naked eye. Under dark skies it is wider than six full Moons, though binoculars and small scopes show mostly its bright core. Look for M32 and M110, its two brightest companions.
M31.howToFind: Find the Great Square of Pegasus. From its top-left star (Alpheratz), follow the line of stars in Andromeda to Mirach, turn toward Cassiopeia to Mu Andromedae, and go the same distance again. It is a fuzzy oval smudge, even visible to the naked eye in dark skies.

M33.about: A face-on spiral whose light is spread thinly, so it is a classic 'faint but big' target that needs dark skies and low power. Averted vision brings out its brighter core and sometimes a hint of spiral arms in larger scopes.
M33.howToFind: Look about halfway between Mirach (in Andromeda) and Alpha Trianguli, the brightest star of the small triangle below it. It is large and faint, so use the lowest power and a dark sky.

M32.about: A small, very dense companion of the Andromeda Galaxy, sitting just south of M31's core. It looks like a fuzzy star with a bright centre and is easy to find with the core of M31 as a guide.
M32.howToFind: Centre on the bright core of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). M32 is the small, round, star-like fuzz just south (toward the bottom of the view in a typical eyepiece) of the core, hugging the edge of M31's glow.

M110.about: The other bright companion of the Andromeda Galaxy, lying northwest of M31. It is much lower in surface brightness than M32, so it is a subtle oval glow that needs dark skies.
M110.howToFind: Centre on the core of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). M110 is a faint oval glow on the opposite side from M32, north-west of M31's core, about half a degree away. It needs a dark sky.

M81.about: A bright, grand-design spiral that a small scope shows as an oval glow with a brighter core. It shares a low-power field with the Cigar Galaxy (M82), so the pair is a favourite.
M81.howToFind: Find the Big Dipper. Draw a line from Phecda (bottom-left of the bowl) through Dubhe (top-right) and continue about the same distance again, roughly 10 degrees. M81 and M82 sit together there.

facts.label: Star formation
facts.value: Roughly 10x faster than the Milky Way

M82.about: A thin, edge-on galaxy being stirred into a burst of star formation by a close pass of M81. It looks like a stretched streak of light, with dark dust lanes visible in larger scopes.
M82.howToFind: Find the Big Dipper. Draw a line from Phecda (bottom-left of the bowl) through Dubhe (top-right) and continue about the same distance again, roughly 10 degrees. M82 is the thin streak just north of the brighter M81.

facts.label: Group
facts.value: Leo Triplet, with M65 and NGC 3628

M66.about: The brightest member of the Leo Triplet, an oval glow with a bright core. It fits in the same field as M65 and NGC 3628 in a wide-field scope.
M66.howToFind: Find Denebola, the bright star at the tail of Leo. M66 is about 7 degrees west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Group
facts.value: Leo Triplet, with M66 and NGC 3628

M65.about: A tilted spiral, more elongated and slightly fainter than M66, in the same wide-field view. Its dust lane needs a big scope.
M65.howToFind: Find Denebola, the bright star at the tail of Leo. M65 is about 7 degrees west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Feature
facts.value: Prominent dust lane, huge central bulge

M104.about: The Sombrero is seen nearly edge-on with a bright bulge and a dark dust lane. Small scopes show an oval glow with a bright core; the dust lane appears in larger apertures with steady skies.
M104.howToFind: Find Algorab, a star in Corvus, the small kite of stars just south-west of Spica. M104 is about 5 degrees north-east of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M63.about: A bright oval core with a faint, diffuse halo. Photographs show a sunflower-like pattern of flocculent spiral arms, but visually it is a soft elongated glow.
M63.howToFind: Find Cor Caroli, the brightest star of Canes Venatici, which forms a triangle with Arcturus and the Big Dipper's handle. M63 is about 5 degrees north-east of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Companion
facts.value: NGC 5195, which it is interacting with

M51.about: The Whirlpool is the first galaxy where spiral structure was seen. Visually it is two fuzzy patches, M51 and its companion NGC 5195, joined by a faint bridge in dark skies and larger scopes.
M51.howToFind: Find Alkaid, the end star of the Big Dipper's handle, and move about 3.5 degrees south-west (down and toward Cor Caroli). Look for a round fuzzy patch with a smaller one touching it.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Large and face-on, so very low surface brightness

M101.about: A huge, face-on spiral that looks very faint through an eyepiece because its light is spread over a large area. It is a good test of sky darkness and averted vision.
M101.howToFind: It forms a triangle with Mizar and Alkaid, the last two stars of the Big Dipper's handle. It is large and faint, so use a dark sky and low power.

facts.label: Feature
facts.value: Dark dust lane in front of the core; the outer gas rotates backwards

M64.about: The Black Eye Galaxy has a bright oval glow with a dark crescent of dust visible in medium scopes under good skies.
M64.howToFind: Find Vindemiatrix, the brightest star in Virgo's upraised arm, north-west of Spica. M64 is about 11 degrees north of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Feature
facts.value: Bright inner ring, outer ring faint

M94.about: A compact galaxy with an unusually bright core and a faint halo. Small scopes see mostly the glowing centre.
M94.howToFind: Find Cor Caroli, the brightest star of Canes Venatici, which forms a triangle with Arcturus and the Big Dipper's handle. M94 is about 3 degrees north of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M106.about: A large, relatively bright spiral that sits alone in a quiet part of the sky. The core is easy, the elongated halo needs darker skies.
M106.howToFind: Find Chara, the second-brightest star of Canes Venatici, just north-west of Cor Caroli. M106 is about 6 degrees north-west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

NGC 4565.about: The Needle is a thin edge-on galaxy, one of the best of its kind. Through a scope it appears as a long, razor-thin streak with a brighter centre.
NGC 4565.howToFind: Find Cor Caroli, the brightest star of Canes Venatici, which forms a triangle with Arcturus and the Big Dipper's handle. NGC 4565 is about 13 degrees south of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Has a supermassive black hole, the first one imaged (2019)

M87.about: The giant at the heart of the Virgo Cluster. It looks like a plain round glow with a brighter centre, but hosts a black hole about 6.5 billion times the Sun's mass.
M87.howToFind: Find Vindemiatrix, the brightest star in Virgo's upraised arm, north-west of Spica. M87 is about 8 degrees west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

NGC 891.about: A thin edge-on galaxy with a dark dust lane that bisects it. A challenge for small scopes, it needs a dark sky and averted vision.
NGC 891.howToFind: Find Almach, the last bright star in that line of stars leading away from the Great Square of Pegasus. NGC 891 is about 3 degrees east of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Feature
facts.value: Distorted by interactions with nearby galaxies

NGC 4631.about: The Whale Galaxy is a long, edge-on galaxy that looks like a streak of light, with a nearby companion, NGC 4627, forming its 'tail'.
NGC 4631.howToFind: Find Cor Caroli, the brightest star of Canes Venatici, which forms a triangle with Arcturus and the Big Dipper's handle. NGC 4631 is about 6 degrees south-west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M74.about: The Phantom Galaxy is a perfect face-on spiral that is very hard to see, because its light is spread so thin. It is often called one of the toughest Messier objects.
M74.howToFind: Find Hamal, the brightest star in Aries, between the Pleiades and the Great Square of Pegasus. M74 is about 11 degrees south-west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

NGC 253.about: A big, elongated galaxy in the southern sky that reaches decent altitude only from low latitudes. It's a bright, spectacular object in dark skies.
NGC 253.howToFind: Find Diphda, the brightest star in the dim sky south of the Great Square of Pegasus. NGC 253 is about 7 degrees south of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Often called a twin of the Milky Way

NGC 7331.about: A tilted spiral that looks like a faint elongated glow. Nearby are the tiny Stephan's Quintet galaxies, which need a large scope.
NGC 7331.howToFind: Find Scheat, the top-right corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. NGC 7331 is about 9 degrees north-west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Has hosted 10 observed supernovae, giving it the Fireworks name

NGC 6946.about: A nearly face-on galaxy sitting in a rich star field, so it appears as a faint glow that is easy to lose among the foreground stars.
NGC 6946.howToFind: Find Alderamin, the brightest star in Cepheus, a shape like a child's drawing of a house, east of Cassiopeia. NGC 6946 is about 6 degrees south-west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M108.about: A long, thin, edge-on galaxy that is a challenge for small scopes. It lies near the Owl Nebula (M97).
M108.howToFind: Find Merak, the other 'pointer' star, at the bottom of the Big Dipper's bowl. M108 is about 1.5 degrees south-east of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M109.about: A faint barred spiral lying near the bright star Phecda in the Big Dipper, which makes it easy to find but hard to see.
M109.howToFind: Find Phecda, the bottom-left star of the Big Dipper's bowl, the one closest to the handle. M109 is about 0.6 degrees south-east of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M77.about: A bright, compact core and a faint disk. It's one of the brightest Seyfert galaxies in the sky.
M77.howToFind: Find Menkar, the nose of Cetus the sea monster. M77 is about 6 degrees south-west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Brightest galaxy of the Virgo Cluster

M49.about: The first Virgo Cluster member found. It's a round glow that brightens toward the centre.
M49.howToFind: Find Vindemiatrix, the brightest star in Virgo's upraised arm, north-west of Spica. M49 is about 9 degrees west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Group
facts.value: Markarian's Chain in the Virgo Cluster

M84.about: A bright round galaxy at the heart of Markarian's Chain, which also includes M86.
M84.howToFind: Find Denebola, the bright star at the tail of Leo. M84 is about 9 degrees east of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

facts.label: Group
facts.value: Markarian's Chain in the Virgo Cluster

M86.about: A round, bright galaxy next to M84. They fit in the same eyepiece field and are the heart of Markarian's Chain.
M86.howToFind: Find Vindemiatrix, the brightest star in Virgo's upraised arm, north-west of Spica. M86 is about 9 degrees west of it. Use your lowest power, let your eyes adjust for a few minutes, and look slightly to the side of it so it appears.

M3.about: A big, bright, round ball of stars. Small scopes show a fuzzy glow with a bright centre; larger scopes begin to resolve the outer stars.
M3.howToFind: Look about halfway between Arcturus and Cor Caroli. It looks like a fuzzy star in binoculars.

M5.about: One of the finest globulars. It is bright and obvious even in small scopes, and it has a lovely pair of stars nearby (5 Serpentis).
M5.howToFind: Start at Unukalhai (Serpens) and move about 6 degrees south-west. The star 5 Serpentis sits right next to the cluster.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the nearest globulars; contains a white dwarf and a pulsar

M4.about: Near the red supergiant Antares. It's loose, large and its stars resolve easily, but its low altitude from mid-northern latitudes makes it dimmer than it should be.
M4.howToFind: It is the easiest of all: M4 is about 1.3 degrees west of Antares, the red heart of Scorpius.

M13.about: The Great Hercules Cluster, the northern sky's best-known globular. A small scope shows a bright fuzzy ball, and a 6-inch begins to speckle with stars. In 1974 a radio message was sent toward it.
M13.howToFind: Find the Keystone, the box of four stars in Hercules, about a third of the way from Vega to Arcturus. M13 sits on the west side of the box, about one third of the way from Eta to Zeta Herculis. It is visible as a faint fuzzy star in binoculars.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the oldest known globulars

M92.about: A little smaller than M13 but just as dense, and easily overlooked because of its famous neighbour in Hercules.
M92.howToFind: Find M13 in the Keystone of Hercules, then move about 9 degrees north-north-east. It forms a triangle with Iota and Eta Herculis.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Contains a planetary nebula and black-hole candidates

M22.about: One of the closest, brightest globulars. It's low in northern skies, but from a clear southern horizon it's spectacular.
M22.howToFind: Find the Teapot of Sagittarius. M22 is about 2.5 degrees north-east of Kaus Borealis, the top star of the Teapot's lid.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Very dense core; a planetary nebula (Pease 1) lies within

M15.about: A tightly packed globular whose core is hard to resolve. It's bright and compact, an easy find near the star Enif.
M15.howToFind: Find Enif, the nose of Pegasus. M15 is about 4 degrees north-west of it, a fuzzy star in binoculars.

M2.about: A rich, dense, round globular in Aquarius, bright and compact in a small scope but not resolved in small apertures.
M2.howToFind: Find Sadalsuud (Beta Aquarii) and go about 5 degrees north.

M12.about: A loose, easily-resolved globular, sitting a few degrees from M10. It has a less compressed core than most, so it looks mottled in medium scopes.
M12.howToFind: Find Unukalhai, the brightest star of Serpens' head, about two fists south of the Northern Crown. M12 is about 18 degrees south-east of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

M10.about: A bright globular in Ophiuchus that makes a nice pair with M12 in wide fields.
M10.howToFind: Find Rasalhague, the star at Ophiuchus's head, about 15 degrees west of Altair. M10 is about 19 degrees south-west of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

M14.about: A fairly faint globular, noticeably dimmer than M10 and M12, which sit nearby in the same constellation.
M14.howToFind: Find Rasalhague, the star at Ophiuchus's head, about 15 degrees west of Altair. M14 is about 16 degrees south of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the most oblate (flattened) globulars

M19.about: An oval-shaped globular, an easy find near the heart of the Milky Way. It is low in northern skies.
M19.howToFind: Find Antares, the bright red heart of Scorpius. M19 is about 7 degrees east of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

M9.about: A small, compact globular close to the centre of the Milky Way. It's easy to find but low from mid-northern latitudes.
M9.howToFind: Find Antares, the bright red heart of Scorpius. M9 is about 14 degrees north-east of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the densest globulars in the Milky Way

M80.about: A dense, bright globular between Antares and Beta Scorpii. It's one of the more compact ones, so it shows a bright core.
M80.howToFind: Find Dschubba, the brightest of the three stars that form Scorpius's head, above Antares. M80 is about 4 degrees east of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

M55.about: A large, sparse globular in Sagittarius whose stars resolve in medium scopes. It's low in northern skies.
M55.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M55 is about 17 degrees east of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Actually belongs to the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, not the Milky Way

M54.about: One of the most distant globulars in Messier's list. It's a bright, compact core that looks like a fuzzy star.
M54.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M54 is about 8 degrees south-east of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Among the farthest globulars in the Messier list

M53.about: A compact, round globular near the star Alpha Comae Berenices, found by star-hopping.
M53.howToFind: Find Vindemiatrix, the brightest star in Virgo's upraised arm, north-west of Spica. M53 is about 8 degrees north of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

M28.about: A bright, compact globular near the Lagoon Nebula and the Teapot's spout.
M28.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M28 is about 0.9 degrees north-west of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

M30.about: A compact globular in Capricornus with a bright core. It's low from northern skies.
M30.howToFind: Find Sadalsuud, the brightest star in Aquarius, in the dim stretch of sky south of Pegasus. M30 is about 18 degrees south of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Sits in a rich Milky Way star field

M56.about: A faint, small globular sitting between Albireo and Gamma Lyrae.
M56.howToFind: Find Albireo, the star at the head of Cygnus the Swan. M56 is about 4 degrees north-west of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Sparse; was once classified as an open cluster

M71.about: A loose, faint globular in Sagitta. It's rich in field stars and hard to tell from an open cluster.
M71.howToFind: Find Altair, the bright star at the south corner of the Summer Triangle, with a fainter star on each side. M71 is about 10 degrees north of it. It looks like a fuzzy star at first. Use medium power to see it as a round, grainy ball.

facts.label: Colour
facts.value: Hot blue stars with a faint reflection nebula

M45.about: The Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, is the most famous star cluster in the sky and visible to the naked eye from even bright cities. It looks best in binoculars or at the lowest power in a scope.
M45.howToFind: No tools needed: look for a tiny dipper-shaped group of stars about 12 degrees (a fist) north-west of Aldebaran, in Taurus. Binoculars show hundreds of stars.

Mel 20.about: A very large, sparse, bright cluster surrounding Mirfak. It's too big for most scopes but great in binoculars.
Mel 20.howToFind: Find Mirfak, the brightest star in Perseus, in the curved line of stars between Cassiopeia and the Pleiades. Mel 20 is about 0.4 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: Two open clusters (h and Chi Persei)

NGC 869/884.about: The Double Cluster is one of the most beautiful star groups in the sky. Visible to the naked eye as a hazy patch, it looks best at low power where both clusters fit in the field.
NGC 869/884.howToFind: Find Cassiopeia's W and Perseus. The Double Cluster lies midway between them as a fuzzy patch you can see with the naked eye in dark skies. Binoculars or low power show two bright clusters side by side.

Cr 399.about: Brocchi's Cluster, the Coathanger, is a chance alignment of stars that looks like an upside-down coat hanger. It's too big for most telescopes but ideal for binoculars.
Cr 399.howToFind: Look halfway between Vega and Altair for a line of six stars with a hook, like a coat hanger hung upside down. Binoculars show it best.

M44.about: The Beehive, also called Praesepe, is a naked-eye cluster in Cancer that Galileo first resolved into stars. It's best in binoculars or a wide-field scope.
M44.howToFind: In a dark sky it looks like a fuzzy patch with the naked eye, halfway between Pollux (in Gemini) and Regulus (in Leo), in the dim constellation Cancer. Binoculars show it as a swarm of stars.

Mel 111.about: The Coma Star Cluster is a huge, sparse cluster of stars that is visible to the naked eye in dark skies. It's very close and spans over 4 degrees, so it's a binocular target.
Mel 111.howToFind: Find Cor Caroli, the brightest star of Canes Venatici, which forms a triangle with Arcturus and the Big Dipper's handle. Mel 111 is about 14 degrees south-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Nearest open cluster to the Sun

Mel 25.about: The Hyades is the V-shaped head of Taurus the Bull. Aldebaran is not a member, just along the line of sight.
Mel 25.howToFind: Find Aldebaran, the orange eye of Taurus. The Hyades is the large V of stars it appears to sit in. Binoculars are best.

M34.about: A bright, loose cluster in Perseus that is visible to the naked eye in dark skies, and is rich in binoculars.
M34.howToFind: Find Algol, the 'Demon Star' in Perseus, south of Mirfak. M34 is about 5 degrees west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M35.about: A big, rich cluster at the foot of Gemini. It has a fainter, more distant neighbour, NGC 2158, in the same eyepiece.
M35.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. M35 is about 10 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M36.about: One of the three bright Auriga clusters, along with M37 and M38. It's a compact, young group.
M36.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. M36 is about 6 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M37.about: The brightest and richest of the Auriga trio, packed with stars like salt and pepper. It's a hazy glow in binoculars and a sparkle in a scope.
M37.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. M37 is about 7 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M38.about: A loose cluster in a pi shape or starfish pattern. A faint companion, NGC 1907, is nearby.
M38.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. M38 is about 7 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M39.about: A large, sparse cluster in Cygnus. It's best at low power or in binoculars, where it forms a triangle of stars.
M39.howToFind: Find Deneb, the star at the tail of Cygnus, at the top of the Summer Triangle. M39 is about 9 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M41.about: A bright cluster less than 5 degrees below Sirius, easily found in binoculars. It has a few orange giants.
M41.howToFind: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the whole sky, below and to the left of Orion's Belt. M41 is about 4 degrees south of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M46.about: A dense, rich cluster in Puppis. The planetary nebula is a foreground object that appears inside it.
M46.howToFind: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the whole sky, below and to the left of Orion's Belt. M46 is about 14 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M47.about: A bright, loose cluster in Puppis visible to the naked eye in dark skies. It sits next to the richer M46.
M47.howToFind: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the whole sky, below and to the left of Orion's Belt. M47 is about 13 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M48.about: A big, sparse cluster in Hydra, bright in binoculars and a good low-power target.
M48.howToFind: Find Procyon, the bright star to the lower left of Orion, which forms a triangle with Betelgeuse and Sirius. M48 is about 14 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M50.about: A heart-shaped cluster in Monoceros. It's easy to find halfway between Sirius and Procyon.
M50.howToFind: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the whole sky, below and to the left of Orion's Belt. M50 is about 9 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M52.about: A rich, compact cluster in Cassiopeia, easily found by extending a line through Alpha and Beta Cassiopeiae. It lies near the Bubble Nebula.
M52.howToFind: Find Caph, the star at the end of Cassiopeia's W that is nearest Andromeda. M52 is about 6 degrees north-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the oldest known open clusters

M67.about: An old, rich cluster in Cancer that has survived far longer than most. It's a hazy patch in binoculars and a mass of faint stars in a telescope.
M67.howToFind: Find Regulus, the bright star at the bottom of Leo's backwards question mark. M67 is about 19 degrees west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M93.about: A compact, triangular cluster in Puppis, easy to find with binoculars.
M93.howToFind: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the whole sky, below and to the left of Orion's Belt. M93 is about 16 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M103.about: A tiny cluster at the end of Cassiopeia, close to Delta Cassiopeiae. A scope shows a triangle of brighter stars.
M103.howToFind: Find Segin, the star at the far end of Cassiopeia's W. M103 is about 4 degrees south-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M6.about: The Butterfly Cluster is a naked-eye cluster in Scorpius shaped like a butterfly's wings. It's low in northern skies.
M6.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M6 is about 12 degrees south-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M7.about: Ptolemy's Cluster is a bright, naked-eye cluster in the tail of Scorpius, known since antiquity. It's low from northern latitudes.
M7.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M7 is about 12 degrees south-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M11.about: The Wild Duck Cluster is one of the richest, most compact open clusters. Its stars form a V like a flock of ducks.
M11.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M11 is about 20 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Sits in the Sagittarius star clouds

M18.about: A small, sparse cluster between M17 and M24. It can be hard to tell from the star background.
M18.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M18 is about 9 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M21.about: A young cluster just northeast of the Trifid Nebula. It's an easy partner to M20 in a low-power view.
M21.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M21 is about 6 degrees north-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M23.about: A big, rich cluster that lies near the Teapot's spout and is easy in binoculars.
M23.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M23 is about 10 degrees north-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M24.about: The Sagittarius Star Cloud is a bright patch of the Milky Way. It's not a cluster but a gap in the dust that shows the dense stars beyond, a spectacular sight in binoculars.
M24.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M24 is about 7 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Contains a Cepheid variable, U Sagittarii

M25.about: A bright, scattered cluster in Sagittarius. It's visible to the naked eye in dark skies.
M25.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M25 is about 6 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M26.about: A small, faint cluster in Scutum, found next to the Wild Duck Cluster (M11).
M26.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M26 is about 17 degrees north of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

M29.about: The Cooling Tower is a small, tight group of stars in Cygnus, found near Sadr.
M29.howToFind: Find Sadr, the star at the centre of the Northern Cross in Cygnus. M29 is about 1.8 degrees south of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 457.about: The Owl or ET Cluster has two bright stars that look like eyes. It's one of the nicest clusters in Cassiopeia.
NGC 457.howToFind: Find Schedar, the brightest star in the W of Cassiopeia. NGC 457 is about 5 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 663.about: A rich cluster in Cassiopeia, easily found in the Cassiopeia clusters hop.
NGC 663.howToFind: Find Segin, the star at the far end of Cassiopeia's W. NGC 663 is about 3 degrees south of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 129.about: A loose group in Cassiopeia best at low power.
NGC 129.howToFind: Find Caph, the star at the end of Cassiopeia's W that is nearest Andromeda. NGC 129 is about 3 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 225.about: The Sailboat Cluster is a sparse group of stars in Cassiopeia, near Gamma Cassiopeiae.
NGC 225.howToFind: Find Caph, the star at the end of Cassiopeia's W that is nearest Andromeda. NGC 225 is about 5 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 752.about: A big, sparse, old cluster in Andromeda. It's best seen in binoculars or a wide-field scope.
NGC 752.howToFind: Find Almach, the last bright star in that line of stars leading away from the Great Square of Pegasus. NGC 752 is about 5 degrees south of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Starts Kemble's Cascade, a line of stars

NGC 1502.about: A tight cluster in Camelopardalis, at the head of the long star chain called Kemble's Cascade.
NGC 1502.howToFind: Find Mirfak, the brightest star in Perseus, in the curved line of stars between Cassiopeia and the Pleiades. NGC 1502 is about 14 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 1647.about: A big, sparse cluster in Taurus, near the Hyades. It's best in binoculars.
NGC 1647.howToFind: Find Aldebaran, the bright orange eye of Taurus the Bull, which you reach by following Orion's Belt up and to the right. NGC 1647 is about 4 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 2129.about: A sparse young cluster in Gemini.
NGC 2129.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. NGC 2129 is about 9 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Feature
facts.value: Looks like a '37' or a chevron

NGC 2169.about: A small cluster in Orion with a distinctive '37' shape, near Xi Orionis.
NGC 2169.howToFind: Find Betelgeuse, the bright orange-red star at Orion's shoulder. NGC 2169 is about 7 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 2232.about: A loose, large cluster in Monoceros that is visible in binoculars.
NGC 2232.howToFind: Find Alnitak, the star at the left end of Orion's Belt (when facing south). NGC 2232 is about 12 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Feature
facts.value: Cone Nebula and Fox Fur Nebula

NGC 2264.about: The Christmas Tree Cluster is a young cluster; the star pattern looks like a tree. The Cone Nebula is a dark-dust and glowing-gas formation at its southern tip.
NGC 2264.howToFind: Find Betelgeuse, the bright orange-red star at Orion's shoulder. NGC 2264 is about 12 degrees east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 2301.about: A loose cluster with chains of stars, in Monoceros.
NGC 2301.howToFind: Find Procyon, the bright star to the lower left of Orion, which forms a triangle with Betelgeuse and Sirius. NGC 2301 is about 13 degrees west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 2362.about: A young cluster around the bright star Tau Canis Majoris. It's a tiny, tight group of stars.
NGC 2362.howToFind: Find Sirius, the brightest star in the whole sky, below and to the left of Orion's Belt. NGC 2362 is about 11 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 6633.about: A bright, scattered cluster in Ophiuchus that makes a nice pair with IC 4756 in binoculars.
NGC 6633.howToFind: Find Rasalhague, the star at Ophiuchus's head, about 15 degrees west of Altair. NGC 6633 is about 14 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the oldest and richest open clusters

NGC 6791.about: A very old, very rich cluster in Lyra that looks faint because it's so distant.
NGC 6791.howToFind: Find Sheliak, one of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra's small parallelogram, below Vega. NGC 6791 is about 8 degrees north-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

NGC 7789.about: Caroline's Rose is a rich old cluster in Cassiopeia whose stars swirl like rose petals.
NGC 7789.howToFind: Find Caph, the star at the end of Cassiopeia's W that is nearest Andromeda. NGC 7789 is about 3 degrees south-west of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

IC 4665.about: The Summer Beehive is a big, sparse cluster in Ophiuchus, best in binoculars.
IC 4665.howToFind: Find Rasalhague, the star at Ophiuchus's head, about 15 degrees west of Altair. IC 4665 is about 7 degrees south of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

IC 4756.about: Graff's Cluster is a huge, sparse cluster in Serpens. It's one of the nicest binocular clusters.
IC 4756.howToFind: Find Rasalhague, the star at Ophiuchus's head, about 15 degrees west of Altair. IC 4756 is about 17 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

Stock 2.about: The Muscle Man Cluster is a big, sparse group in Cassiopeia, near the Double Cluster.
Stock 2.howToFind: Find Segin, the star at the far end of Cassiopeia's W. Stock 2 is about 5 degrees south-east of it. Binoculars or your lowest-power eyepiece work best, since the cluster is bigger than most telescope views.

facts.label: Stars
facts.value: Contains the Trapezium, four hot young stars

M42.about: The Orion Nebula is a star-forming cloud visible to the naked eye as the fuzzy middle star of Orion's sword. In a telescope it shows wings of glowing gas around the Trapezium. It's the brightest nebula in the sky.
M42.howToFind: Find Orion's Belt, the row of three stars. Just below it hangs Orion's sword, three fainter stars in a line; the middle one is the Orion Nebula, which looks fuzzy even to the naked eye.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Part of the Orion Nebula complex

M43.about: De Mairan's Nebula is a small, rounded lobe of the Orion Nebula that is separated from M42 by a dark lane. It's lit by a single young star.
M43.howToFind: Find the Orion Nebula (M42) in Orion's sword. M43 is the small, round patch just north-east of it, separated by a dark lane.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Brightest reflection nebula in the sky

M78.about: A reflection nebula in Orion whose gas and dust reflect the light of nearby stars. It's faint and fuzzy, with two stars embedded in it.
M78.howToFind: Find Alnitak, the star at the left end of Orion's Belt (when facing south). M78 is about 3 degrees north-east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Next to Alnitak, the left belt star of Orion

NGC 2024.about: The Flame Nebula is drowned out by the glare of Alnitak, so it needs dark skies and the star kept out of view.
NGC 2024.howToFind: Find Alnitak, the star at the left end of Orion's Belt (when facing south). NGC 2024 is about 0.3 degrees east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: Emission nebula, backdrop of the Horsehead Nebula

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: The Horsehead (Barnard 33) is a dark cloud silhouetted against it

IC 434.about: A faint glow that lights the famous Horsehead Nebula. It's one of the hardest visual targets and normally needs an H-beta filter and a dark sky.
IC 434.howToFind: Find Alnitak, the star at the left end of Orion's Belt (when facing south). IC 434 is about 0.5 degrees south of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 2175.about: The Monkey Head Nebula is a faint glow in Orion around a young cluster, NGC 2175. It's hard to see visually.
NGC 2175.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. NGC 2175 is about 13 degrees south-east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 2237.about: The Rosette Nebula is a huge ring of glowing gas around a young cluster. Its faint ring needs dark skies and a filter. The cluster at its centre is easy.
NGC 2237.howToFind: Find Betelgeuse, the bright orange-red star at Orion's shoulder. NGC 2237 is about 10 degrees east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 1499.about: The California Nebula is huge and very faint, so it needs a dark sky and a hydrogen-beta filter. It's a great camera target.
NGC 1499.howToFind: Find Algol, the 'Demon Star' in Perseus, south of Mirfak. NGC 1499 is about 11 degrees south-east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Lit by the star AE Aurigae

IC 405.about: The Flaming Star Nebula is a faint cloud around a runaway star in Auriga, hard to see visually.
IC 405.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. IC 405 is about 6 degrees north of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

M8.about: The Lagoon Nebula is a large star-forming region in Sagittarius, visible to the naked eye from a dark site. Binoculars show its glow and a cluster in the middle.
M8.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M8 is about 6 degrees west of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

M20.about: The Trifid Nebula is split into three parts by dark lanes. It's a faint glow in a small scope, and its colours show up only in photographs.
M20.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M20 is about 6 degrees west of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

M16.about: The Eagle Nebula is a star-forming region in Serpens. The cluster is easy; the nebula and its pillars are best in larger scopes with a filter.
M16.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M16 is about 12 degrees north of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

M17.about: The Omega or Swan Nebula is one of the brightest nebulae. Its bright bar looks like a check mark or a swan in a small scope.
M17.howToFind: Find Kaus Borealis, the star at the top of the Teapot's lid in Sagittarius. M17 is about 9 degrees north of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 7000.about: The North America Nebula looks like the continent in photographs. It's visible as a faint glow to the naked eye in dark skies and needs a wide field and a filter.
NGC 7000.howToFind: Find Deneb, the star at the tail of Cygnus, at the top of the Summer Triangle. NGC 7000 is about 3 degrees east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

IC 5146.about: The Cocoon Nebula is a small, faint nebula in Cygnus with a young cluster at its heart.
IC 5146.howToFind: Find Deneb, the star at the tail of Cygnus, at the top of the Summer Triangle. IC 5146 is about 13 degrees east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 7380.about: The Wizard Nebula is a faint nebula around an open cluster in Cepheus. It's very hard visually.
NGC 7380.howToFind: Find Caph, the star at the end of Cassiopeia's W that is nearest Andromeda. NGC 7380 is about 11 degrees west of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 7023.about: The Iris Nebula is a blue reflection nebula around a bright star in Cepheus. Visually only the star and a faint haze show.
NGC 7023.howToFind: Find Alderamin, the brightest star in Cepheus, a shape like a child's drawing of a house, east of Cassiopeia. NGC 7023 is about 6 degrees north of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

IC 1396.about: A huge, very faint emission nebula in Cepheus containing the Elephant's Trunk dark cloud. It's mostly an astrophotography target.
IC 1396.howToFind: Find Alderamin, the brightest star in Cepheus, a shape like a child's drawing of a house, east of Cassiopeia. IC 1396 is about 6 degrees south-east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

IC 1805.about: The Heart Nebula is a large, faint emission nebula in Cassiopeia. It's dim visually and needs a dark sky.
IC 1805.howToFind: Find Segin, the star at the far end of Cassiopeia's W. IC 1805 is about 5 degrees south-east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

IC 1848.about: The Soul Nebula is next to the Heart Nebula. It's very faint visually.
IC 1848.howToFind: Find Segin, the star at the far end of Cassiopeia's W. IC 1848 is about 7 degrees south-east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

NGC 281.about: The Pacman Nebula is a faint nebula around a small cluster in Cassiopeia.
NGC 281.howToFind: Find Schedar, the brightest star in the W of Cassiopeia. NGC 281 is about 1.7 degrees east of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A bubble blown by a hot star's wind

NGC 7635.about: The Bubble Nebula is a ring of glowing gas next to M52. It's very faint visually and needs a large scope and filter.
NGC 7635.howToFind: Find Caph, the star at the end of Cassiopeia's W that is nearest Andromeda. NGC 7635 is about 6 degrees west of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

M57.about: The Ring Nebula is a shell of gas shed by a dying star. In a small scope at medium power it looks like a smoke ring or a small, faint doughnut, and it's easy to find between Beta and Gamma Lyrae.
M57.howToFind: Find Lyra's small parallelogram below Vega. The Ring Nebula is halfway between its bottom two stars, Beta and Gamma Lyrae.

M27.about: The Dumbbell Nebula is one of the brightest planetary nebulae. It looks like an apple core in a small scope and is easy to see in binoculars from dark skies.
M27.howToFind: Find the little arrow of Sagitta, then look for the 'nose' star Gamma Sagittae. The Dumbbell is about 3 degrees north of it in Vulpecula, easy to find in binoculars.

M97.about: The Owl Nebula is a faint, round planetary nebula. Larger scopes show two dark patches that look like an owl's eyes.
M97.howToFind: Find Merak, the other 'pointer' star, at the bottom of the Big Dipper's bowl. M97 is about 2 degrees south-east of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Bipolar, often called the faintest Messier object

M76.about: The Little Dumbbell is the dimmest object in Messier's list in many lists. It's a small, faint rectangle in a medium scope.
M76.howToFind: Find Almach, the last bright star in that line of stars leading away from the Great Square of Pegasus. M76 is about 10 degrees north of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: One of the nearest planetary nebulae

NGC 7293.about: The Helix Nebula is huge and faint because its light is spread over a large area. It needs a dark sky and a filter. It's low in northern skies.
NGC 7293.howToFind: In Aquarius, low in the south from mid-northern latitudes. Use a sky app to find Delta Aquarii, then look about 7 degrees south-west of it. It is huge and faint, so use binoculars or low power, a filter if you have one, and a dark clear southern horizon.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Very complex structure seen by Hubble

NGC 6543.about: The Cat's Eye Nebula is a tiny planetary nebula. In a small scope it looks like a slightly fuzzy bluish star.
NGC 6543.howToFind: Find Eltanin, the bright star in the head of Draco, about 12 degrees above Vega. NGC 6543 is about 15 degrees north of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Blinks in and out of view with averted vision

NGC 6826.about: The Blinking Planetary appears and disappears as you look straight at it and then away from it, because of the central star.
NGC 6826.howToFind: Find Deneb, the star at the tail of Cygnus, at the top of the Summer Triangle. NGC 6826 is about 11 degrees north-west of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

NGC 7662.about: The Blue Snowball is a small, round planetary nebula with a blue-green hue. It looks like a fuzzy star at low power.
NGC 7662.howToFind: Find Scheat, the top-right corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. NGC 7662 is about 15 degrees north of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

NGC 2392.about: The Eskimo Nebula is small and bright, with a central star surrounded by a halo. It needs high magnification to show anything beyond a fuzzy star.
NGC 2392.howToFind: Find Pollux, the brighter of the twin stars of Gemini. NGC 2392 is about 8 degrees south-west of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

NGC 7009.about: The Saturn Nebula has ansae that look like Saturn's rings. In a small scope it's a blue-green oval.
NGC 7009.howToFind: Find Sadalsuud, the brightest star in Aquarius, in the dim stretch of sky south of Pegasus. NGC 7009 is about 9 degrees south-west of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

NGC 3242.about: The Ghost of Jupiter is a bright, oval, bluish disk in Hydra, about the size of Jupiter.
NGC 3242.howToFind: Hydra is the long, faint snake south of Cancer and Leo. Use a sky app to find Mu Hydrae near its head, then look about 2 degrees south of it. At low power it looks like a star; high power shows a small blue-green disc.

NGC 40.about: The Bow-Tie Nebula is a small, faint planetary nebula around a very bright central star.
NGC 40.howToFind: Find Segin, the star at the far end of Cassiopeia's W. NGC 40 is about 13 degrees north-west of it. At low power it looks like a star. Switch to higher power and it will show a small, slightly fuzzy disc.

M1.about: The Crab Nebula is the debris from a star that was seen exploding in 1054 CE. In a small scope it's a faint oval smudge.
M1.howToFind: Find Elnath, the tip of Taurus's northern horn. M1 is about 7 degrees south of it. It is faint, so use a dark sky and, if you have one, an OIII filter.

NGC 6960/92.about: The Veil Nebula is a huge remnant of a supernova that looks like faint wisps. It needs a dark sky and an OIII filter.
NGC 6960/92.howToFind: Find Sadr, the star at the centre of the Northern Cross in Cygnus. NGC 6960/92 is about 11 degrees south-east of it. It is faint, so use a dark sky and, if you have one, an OIII filter.

Albireo.about: The most beautiful double star in the sky, a gold-orange star beside a blue one. It marks the head of Cygnus the Swan and is easy to split at low power.
Albireo.howToFind: Find the Northern Cross in Cygnus; Albireo is the star at the bottom, the swan's beak. The colourful pair splits in even a small telescope.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Its brightness varies across phases; an average magnitude is used here

Moon.about: Earth's only natural satellite. The terminator, the line between day and night, shows the best craters and mountains. A full Moon is bright but flat.
Moon.howToFind: Look up! It is in the sky about half the time. Check the phase: crater detail looks best along the shadow line, not at full Moon.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Always close to the Sun in the sky

Mercury.about: Mercury is small and hard to find, since it never strays far from the Sun. It shows phases like the Moon.
Mercury.howToFind: Very tricky: look low on the horizon about 45 minutes after sunset or before sunrise, when it is at its greatest distance from the Sun.

Venus.about: Venus is brilliant and shows phases in even small telescopes. It looks like a featureless white disk because of its thick clouds.
Venus.howToFind: Look low in the west after sunset or low in the east before sunrise: it is the brightest 'star' in the sky, steady and silvery-white.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Best seen near opposition, every ~26 months

Mars.about: The red planet shows its polar caps and dark markings in a small scope, but only when it's close to Earth.
Mars.howToFind: Look for a steady, orange-red 'star' that does not twinkle. Check a sky app for when it is high and bright.

facts.label: Moons
facts.value: 4 bright Galilean moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto)

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Cloud belts and the Great Red Spot

Jupiter.about: A small telescope shows Jupiter's cloud belts and its four bright moons, which change position nightly.
Jupiter.howToFind: Look for a very bright, steady, cream-white 'star' that is brighter than anything else except Venus. A small scope shows four moons.

facts.label: Moons
facts.value: Titan is visible in small scopes

Saturn.about: The ringed planet is one of the best sights in the sky. Even a small scope shows its rings clearly.
Saturn.howToFind: Look for a steady, yellowish 'star' that does not twinkle. Even a small telescope shows its rings.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Barely visible to the naked eye in dark skies

Uranus.about: A small blue-green dot in a telescope, found only with a chart. It was the first planet found with a telescope (1781).
Uranus.howToFind: You need a sky app to find it: it is a faint dot in a dark sky and looks like a very small bluish-green disc in a telescope.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Not visible to the naked eye

Neptune.about: A tiny blue-grey dot that looks like a star. It needs a chart to find and a medium scope to see a disk.
Neptune.howToFind: You need a sky app and a telescope: it is a faint bluish dot that looks just like a star.

NGC 6888.about: The Crescent Nebula is a shell of gas blown by a massive, dying star. It's faint and needs a dark sky and an OIII filter to show anything beyond a hint of glow.
NGC 6888.howToFind: Find Sadr, the star at the centre of the Northern Cross in Cygnus. NGC 6888 is about 3 degrees south-west of it. Use low power under a dark sky. A nebula filter (UHC or OIII) helps a lot if you have one.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A fast-moving star, an old giant from the Milky Way's halo

Arcturus.about: The brightest star in the northern sky and the fourth brightest overall. Follow the arc of the Big Dipper's handle to find it.
Arcturus.howToFind: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle away from the bowl ('arc to Arcturus'). It is the bright orange star you reach.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Spins so fast it's flattened; has a dusty debris disk

Vega.about: The brightest star in Lyra and the fifth brightest in the sky. It was the north star about 12,000 years ago and will be again in about 13,700 CE.
Vega.howToFind: The brightest star nearly overhead on summer evenings. It is one corner of the Summer Triangle, with Deneb and Altair.

facts.label: Spectral type
facts.value: G8 III + G0 III (two yellow giants)

Capella.about: The sixth brightest star in the sky and the brightest in Auriga. It's actually two pairs of stars, though to the eye it looks like one yellow star.
Capella.howToFind: A bright yellow star in Auriga, high in the northern sky on winter evenings. It is close to the northern horizon in summer.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Has a white dwarf companion that needs a large scope

Procyon.about: The little dog's star. It's one of the closest stars to the Sun and forms the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse.
Procyon.howToFind: Find Orion, then look to the lower left of Betelgeuse. Procyon forms a triangle with Betelgeuse and Sirius.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A semi-regular variable, between mag 0.0 and 1.6

Betelgeuse.about: The red shoulder of Orion, and a star that will eventually explode as a supernova. It dimmed dramatically in 2019-2020.
Betelgeuse.howToFind: The orange-red star marking Orion's shoulder (upper left, when you face south in winter).

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Spins once in ~9 hours, so it's noticeably flattened

Altair.about: The bright star of Aquila and the south corner of the Summer Triangle. It's one of the closest naked-eye stars.
Altair.howToFind: The bright star at the south point of the Summer Triangle, with a fainter star on either side of it.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Has a probable red dwarf companion; a spacecraft, Pioneer 10, is heading its way

Aldebaran.about: The eye of Taurus the Bull. It looks like the brightest star of the Hyades cluster but is not part of it, lying about half as far away.
Aldebaran.howToFind: Follow Orion's Belt up and to the right. The first bright orange star you reach is Aldebaran, the eye of Taurus.

Pollux.about: The brighter of the Gemini twins, slightly brighter than Castor despite its Beta label.
Pollux.howToFind: The brighter of the twin stars of Gemini, above and to the left of Orion. Its twin, Castor, is next to it.

Deneb.about: The tail of Cygnus the Swan and the northeast corner of the Summer Triangle. It's one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye.
Deneb.howToFind: The tail of Cygnus the Swan and the top of the Summer Triangle. Look for the Northern Cross overhead in summer.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Spins in 16 hours, so it's strongly flattened; a multiple star

Regulus.about: The heart of Leo the Lion. It sits almost exactly on the ecliptic, so the Moon and planets pass close to it.
Regulus.howToFind: The bright star at the bottom of Leo's backwards question mark (the 'Sickle'), in spring.

Castor.about: The other twin in Gemini. A small telescope splits it into two bright stars, each of which is itself a double.
Castor.howToFind: The slightly fainter of the Gemini twins, above and to the left of Orion in winter.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Will become a red giant in a few million years

Bellatrix.about: The 'Amazon Star' marking Orion's left shoulder.
Bellatrix.howToFind: Orion's upper-right shoulder star, opposite Betelgeuse.

Elnath.about: The tip of Taurus's northern horn. It was once shared with Auriga.
Elnath.howToFind: The tip of the northern horn of Taurus, about 12 degrees north-east of Aldebaran, shared with Auriga's pentagon.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A magnetic star with unusual abundances

Alioth.about: The brightest star in the Big Dipper, the one closest to the bowl in the handle.
Alioth.howToFind: The bright star in the Big Dipper's handle closest to the bowl.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A binary; the companion needs a telescope

Dubhe.about: One of the pointer stars of the Big Dipper. Following it and Merak leads to Polaris.
Dubhe.howToFind: One of the two 'pointer' stars at the edge of the Big Dipper's bowl. Follow it and Merak to find Polaris.

Mirfak.about: The brightest star in Perseus and the centre of the Alpha Persei Cluster. Sweep it with binoculars.
Mirfak.howToFind: The brightest star in Perseus, in the curved line of stars that leads from Cassiopeia toward the Pleiades.

Alkaid.about: The end of the Big Dipper's handle. Unlike most of the other Dipper stars, it isn't part of the Ursa Major moving group.
Alkaid.howToFind: The star at the very end of the Big Dipper's handle.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Two stars that eclipse each other every 3.96 days

Menkalinan.about: The shoulder of Auriga the Charioteer.
Menkalinan.howToFind: The second-brightest star of Auriga's pentagon, about 7 degrees east of Capella.

Alhena.about: The foot of Pollux in Gemini, found close to the Milky Way.
Alhena.howToFind: In Gemini's foot, about 15 degrees south-west (down and to the right) of Pollux.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A Cepheid variable and part of a triple system

Polaris.about: The North Star, which hardly moves because it lies almost exactly over Earth's north pole. It's not especially bright, just always in the same place.
Polaris.howToFind: Use the two 'pointer' stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl (Merak to Dubhe) and go about five times that distance. It barely moves during the night.

Hamal.about: The brightest star in Aries, the Ram. Its name means 'lamb' in Arabic.
Hamal.howToFind: The brightest star in Aries, in the small crooked line of stars between the Pleiades and the Great Square of Pegasus.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Four stars in Mizar, six counting Alcor

Mizar.about: The middle star in the handle of the Big Dipper. Alcor sits next to it, and together they're a famous naked-eye double; Mizar itself is a telescopic double, the first discovered (1617).
Mizar.howToFind: The middle star in the Big Dipper's handle. Look for its tiny companion, Alcor, right next to it.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A line from Mirach through Mu Andromedae leads to M31

Mirach.about: The middle star in the Andromeda line, used to hop to the Andromeda Galaxy (M31).
Mirach.howToFind: The middle of the three bright stars running from the Great Square of Pegasus into Andromeda. It has a slightly orange tint.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: A chemically peculiar star, rich in mercury and manganese

Alpheratz.about: The star that joins the Great Square of Pegasus to Andromeda, belonging to both.
Alpheratz.howToFind: The top-left corner star of the Great Square of Pegasus, which it shares with Andromeda.

facts.label: Notable
facts.value: Has a close companion, discovered in 1867

Rasalhague.about: The head of Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer. Its name means 'head of the serpent collector.'
Rasalhague.howToFind: A moderately bright star about 15 degrees west of Altair, at the head of Ophiuchus.
